Statistics of trait variation within and among populations

Source: R/population_stats.R
population_stats.Rd

Summarises traits measured on individuals of several populations of each species, such as the output of sample_individuals() or field data, into statistics that carry information on the genetic variance, on drift and on gene flow, for inference by approximate Bayesian computation (abc_table()) next to summary_stats(). Each statistic that lacks its inputs is NA, so the result always has the same names.

Usage

population_stats(
  individuals,
  trait = "trait",
  site = "site",
  species = "species",
  env = "env",
  abundance = NULL,
  step = NULL,
  coords = NULL,
  near = 1.5,
  far = 3,
  by_species = FALSE
)

Arguments

individuals

Data frame with one row per individual.

trait, site, species, env

Names of the columns with the trait (numeric), the site, the species and the environment of the site (numeric), as in the output of sample_individuals().

abundance

Name of a column with the abundance of the population of each individual, one value per population, or NULL (the default), which leaves within_slope, size_cor and temporal_slope as NA.

step

Name of a column with the survey of each individual, or NULL (the default) for a single survey, which leaves temporal, temporal_slope, temporal_step and temporal_step_slope as NA. Without step, all the individuals of a population are pooled.

coords

Matrix or data frame with the coordinates of the sites in two columns and the names of the sites as row names, or NULL (the default), which leaves near, far and dist_cor as NA.

near, far

Distances (non-negative numbers, near no larger than far) that define neighbouring and distant pairs of populations.

by_species

If TRUE, a data frame with the statistics of each species and its weight instead of the averages.

Value

Named numeric vector, or with by_species = TRUE a data frame with one row per species.

Details

A population is a species in a site. The statistics of a species use its populations with at least two individuals measured at the last survey, and need three such populations at sites that differ in environment. slope and r2 are the slope and \(R^2\) of a linear regression of population means on the environment, sd the standard deviation of the means and resid_sd that of the residuals. within is the logarithm of the mean variance within populations (the phenotypic variance, genetic plus environmental) and within_slope the slope of the variance within populations on the logarithm of abundance, positive when drift erodes the genetic variance of small populations. qst is the residual variance among population means, \(V_B\), relative to \(V_B + 2 V_W\), where \(V_W\) is the mean variance within populations, a divergence among populations beyond what the environment explains, in the form of \(Q_{ST}\) (Spitze 1993) but with phenotypes. near and far are the semivariances of residuals between populations closer than near and farther than far, relative to the residual variance, and dist_cor the correlation of squared differences of residuals with distance: drift makes neighbours differ, gene flow makes them alike. size_cor is the correlation of absolute residuals with the logarithm of abundance, negative when small populations drift more.

With two or more surveys (step), the first and the last are compared, in the populations with at least two individuals measured in both. temporal is the mean squared change of population means minus its sampling variance, relative to the variance within populations, and temporal_slope the slope of that corrected change on the inverse of abundance, the basis of the temporal method of estimating the effective size (Waples 1989). Over a long interval, selection and gene flow also move the means, so temporal_step uses every pair of consecutive surveys instead: the mean, over these pairs and their populations measured in both, of the squared change minus its sampling variance, divided by the interval between the surveys (in the units of step, so per generation when a step is a generation) and by the variance within populations at the last survey. It estimates the variance of drift per generation relative to the phenotypic variance, which is about \(G / (N_e (G + V_E))\) (Lande 1976). temporal_step_slope is the slope of the corrected change per unit of time on the inverse of the abundance at the later survey. Both need a numeric step and three changes in all; with two surveys, temporal_step is temporal divided by the interval.

The statistics of each species are averaged over species, weighted by the summed abundance of their populations at the last survey (or by their number of populations without abundance). slope_min and slope_max are the smallest and largest slope among species. Means and variances are those of the measured individuals, so they include sampling error, as field data would; subsample_individuals() changes the effort.

References

Lande, R. (1976). Natural selection and random genetic drift in phenotypic evolution. Evolution, 30, 314–334. doi:10.1111/j.1558-5646.1976.tb00911.x

Spitze, K. (1993). Population structure in Daphnia obtusa: quantitative genetic and allozymic variation. Genetics, 135, 367–374. doi:10.1093/genetics/135.2.367

Waples, R. S. (1989). A generalized approach for estimating effective population size from temporal changes in allele frequency. Genetics, 121, 379–391. doi:10.1093/genetics/121.2.379

Examples

set.seed(1)
land <- landscape_grid(side = 6, env_bandwidth = 2)
traits <- data.frame(optimum = c(30, 50, 70), sigma = 15, r_max = 5,
                     row.names = c("a", "b", "c"))
alpha <- matrix(0.01, 3, 3, dimnames = list(rownames(traits), rownames(traits)))
diag(alpha) <- 0.02
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(land, traits, alpha, dispersal = 0.01, n_steps = 120,
                              record_steps = c(100, 120),
                              evolution = evolution_control(4, ne_ratio = 0.2, env_var = 1))
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 10, source = "evolution", step = c(100, 120))
coords <- land$coords
rownames(coords) <- rownames(sim$abundance)
round(population_stats(ind, abundance = "abundance", step = "step", coords = coords), 3)
#>               slope                  r2                  sd            resid_sd 
#>               0.204               0.218               8.577               7.463 
#>              within        within_slope                 qst                near 
#>               1.596               0.166               0.846               0.976 
#>                 far            dist_cor            size_cor            temporal 
#>               0.920              -0.042              -0.223               0.414 
#>      temporal_slope       temporal_step temporal_step_slope           slope_min 
#>              29.080               0.021               1.454               0.107 
#>           slope_max 
#>               0.350
